subject: Statistics 1 · Foundation
title: Describing categorical data

intro.text: Start from everyday examples. Read the diagrams, work through the steps, and try the questions before revealing the answers.

blocks.text: A frequency is a count. A frequency distribution lists the different categories and how many observations belong to each. It turns a long list of labels into a short, useful summary.

blocks.alt: The lecture’s first list becomes counts A = 4, B = 2, C = 2, D = 2.
blocks.caption: The lecture’s first list becomes counts A = 4, B = 2, C = 2, D = 2.

blocks.text: Build a table one observation at a time
Use the list A, A, B, C, A, D, A, B, D, C. First list the distinct categories A, B, C and D. Next read each observation once and add a tally in the matching row. Finally count the tallies.

The total number of observations is often written n. Here n = 10, and 4 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10. For this single-response variable, each case belongs to exactly one category. Categories should not overlap or leave observed values out.
The lecture’s practice lists, counted carefully

Source clarification: the opening exercise slide in Lecture 2.1 prints a different third list, A,A,B,C,A,A,B,B,D,C,A,B,C,D,B. That list has A = 5, B = 5, C = 3, D = 2. The later worked table uses the third list shown above, with counts 3,6,3,3. Always count the actual list you are given.
A spreadsheet method

A pivot table can do the same counting: use the category as the row field and count the category entries as the value. Check that the result counts text entries rather than trying to sum them, and check whether blanks were included. The exact menu position depends on the spreadsheet app.

blocks.answer: 4 + 3 + 2 = 9. If the total is different, check for a missed or duplicated observation.

Raw counts can be hard to compare when groups have different sizes. Relative frequency tells us what fraction of a group belongs to a category.

blocks.alt: Divide each count by the number of observations to get a share.
blocks.caption: Divide each count by the number of observations to get a share.

blocks.text: One idea, three ways to write it

For A in the first lecture example, f = 4 and n = 10. Its relative frequency is 4/10 = 0.4, its proportion is 0.4, and its percentage is 40%. The remaining three categories each have 2/10 = 0.2 = 20%.
Why the denominator matters

Lists 1 and 2 have different counts but identical proportions: A is 40% in both. As another example, 20 bus users among 50 students is 40%, whereas 30 among 100 is 30%. The second group has more bus users but a smaller share.
Checks that catch mistakes

Each relative frequency lies between 0 and 1. For a complete set of non-overlapping categories, exact relative frequencies sum to 1 and exact percentages sum to 100%. Use the total for the group you are actually describing: after filtering, the denominator may change.

Keep fractions or full precision while calculating and round only for display. Three equal categories each have share 1/3. Displaying each as 33.3% gives 99.9%; this small discrepancy is rounding, not a missing observation.

blocks.question: A category has 12 of 40 responses. Find its relative frequency and percentage.
blocks.text: A category has 12 of 40 responses. Find its relative frequency and percentage. Answer: 12/40 = 0.3 = 30%.

blocks.question: Group X has 8 out of 20 choosing A. Group Y has 15 out of 50 choosing A. Which has a larger share?
blocks.answer: X: 8/20 = 40%. Y: 15/50 = 30%. X has the larger share even though Y has the larger count.
blocks.text: Group X has 8 out of 20 choosing A. Group Y has 15 out of 50 choosing A. Which has a larger share? Answer: X: 8/20 = 40%. Y: 15/50 = 30%. X has the larger share even though Y has the larger count.

blocks.question: In a class of 25 students, 10 choose football. Find the relative frequency and percentage.
blocks.answer: Relative frequency = 10/25 = 0.4. Percentage = 0.4×100% = 40%. Use the class total 25 as the denominator.

blocks.answer: 5/20 = 0.25 = 25%. The question asks within the filtered class, so divide by 20, not by the original 100.

sections.title: Pie charts: show parts of one whole

blocks.text: A pie chart is a circle split into slices. Each slice has an area proportional to its category’s share. The entire circle represents the whole group, or 100%.

blocks.alt: A 40% share uses 144 degrees; each 20% share uses 72 degrees.
blocks.caption: A 40% share uses 144 degrees; each 20% share uses 72 degrees.

blocks.text: From a table to a circle
Start with a relative-frequency table. Multiply each share by 360° to get its slice angle. Draw the slices using a protractor, then label each category and its share.
With counts 6,3,3,3 out of 15, the slices are exactly the same: 40%,20%,20%,20%. A pie shows proportions, so different group sizes can produce the same pie.
Read the slice, not just its color
Half the circle is 50% or 180°. A share greater than 50% occupies more than half. In this example A is the largest category but is not a majority: 40% is less than 50%.
When a pie chart helps

A pie works best for a few categories that form one whole, especially when showing that a category is more than half. Comparing nearly equal slices is difficult; a bar chart usually makes small differences clearer. Avoid a pie for overlapping multiple-response categories because their percentages may exceed 100%.
Make it in a spreadsheet

Prepare category and count columns. Select the summary table without its Total row, insert a chart, and choose a pie chart. Label slices with category and percentage. Check that the chart represents the same group as the table and that no category was omitted.

blocks.question: A category has 9 of 30 observations. What angle should its slice have?
blocks.text: A category has 9 of 30 observations. What angle should its slice have? Answer: 9/30 = 0.3, so the slice is 0.3 × 360° = 108°.

blocks.question: The largest category is 45%. Is it a majority?
blocks.answer: No. It is the largest share, but a majority requires more than 50%.
blocks.text: The largest category is 45%. Is it a majority? Answer: No. It is the largest share, but a majority requires more than 50%.

blocks.answer: 25% = 0.25. Angle = 0.25×360° = 90°, one quarter of a circle.

blocks.answer: 180/360 = 0.5 = 50%. It represents half the whole, not more than half.

sections.title: Bar charts, Pareto charts and category order

blocks.text: A bar chart compares categories using bar lengths. You can display counts, relative frequencies, or percentages. Tell the reader which one the axis uses.

blocks.alt: Separate, equal-width bars show category counts from a zero baseline.
blocks.caption: Separate, equal-width bars show category counts from a zero baseline.

blocks.text: Build a bar chart

Start with the frequency table. Put category names on one axis and frequency on the other. Use equal-width bars, leave gaps between them, and make each bar height match its count. Label the variable, the measurement axis, and the group being summarized. Horizontal bars are useful for long category names.

For counts 4,2,2,2, A’s bar is twice as high as each other bar. A relative-frequency chart would use heights 0.4,0.2,0.2,0.2. A percentage chart would use 40,20,20,20. The pattern is the same because all values use the same denominator.
Pareto: sort by descending frequency

blocks.alt: The Pareto order is B, A, C, D for counts 6,4,3,2.
blocks.caption: The Pareto order is B, A, C, D for counts 6,4,3,2.

blocks.text: A Pareto chart is a bar chart arranged from highest frequency to lowest. It helps identify the most common problem or category, for example the defect that needs attention first. For the lecture list A,B,B,C,A,D,B,B,A,C,B,B,C,D,A, counts are A = 4, B = 6, C = 3 and D = 2.
Source clarification: the lecture displays A as 0.26 and D as 0.14. For the stated counts, the correct shares are 4/15 ≈ 0.2667 and 2/15 ≈ 0.1333. Use the counts to calculate accurately.
Ordinal categories keep their natural order

The lecture’s 20 T-shirt sizes are L,M,M,S,L,S,S,M,L,M,M,S,S,L,M,S,M,S,L,M. Counts are Small = 7, Medium = 8, Large = 5, giving 35%,40%,25%. Keep S,M,L on the axis rather than sorting M,S,L by frequency. Order is part of the information.

rows: Show shares of one whole with few categories
Find the most frequent unordered problems

blocks.question: Complaints are Delivery = 8, Payment = 3, Quality = 11. What is the Pareto order?
blocks.answer: Quality (11), Delivery (8), Payment (3).
blocks.text: Complaints are Delivery = 8, Payment = 3, Quality = 11. What is the Pareto order? Answer: Quality (11), Delivery (8), Payment (3).

blocks.answer: For an ordinal bar chart, preserve Poor, Fair, Good, Excellent so the ranking remains visible.

sections.title: Read charts carefully: avoid misleading graphs

blocks.text: A chart should make the data easier to understand. Its appearance should not exaggerate a difference, hide a category, or make a different group look like the one you meant.

blocks.alt: Counts of 100 and 110 differ by 10%; a baseline of 90 makes the bars look twice as tall.
blocks.caption: Counts of 100 and 110 differ by 10%; a baseline of 90 makes the bars look twice as tall.

blocks.text: Begin with the purpose and the labels

Use a pie to show parts of a whole and a bar chart to compare groups. Name the categories and say whether the values are counts, shares, or percentages. State which cases are included. If only one intake or one region is shown, put that in the title or caption.
Too many categories can hide the message

When there are many small categories, a chart becomes hard to read. You may group some as “Other”, but explain what it contains and keep the underlying counts available. Do not silently omit inconvenient categories. Keep important distinctions when they matter to the question.
The area principle

blocks.alt: Visible area should grow in proportion to the count, and labels and totals must remain honest.
blocks.caption: Visible area should grow in proportion to the count, and labels and totals must remain honest.

blocks.text: The area principle says the amount of visible area should match the amount of data. If a count doubles, doubling both the width and height of an icon multiplies its area by four, exaggerating the change. Equal-width bars avoid this problem because their areas grow with their heights. Decorative bottles, pictures, 3D slices and perspective can distort comparisons.
Truncated axes can exaggerate differences

For North = 100 and South = 110, South is 10% larger. If a bar axis starts at 90, visible heights are 10 and 20, which look twice as large. A zero baseline gives the correct bar-length comparison. This is why bar charts should normally start at zero.

If an axis is shortened or broken, show a clear break symbol and explain the scale change. A break warns the reader; it does not make bar lengths proportional again. For an ordinary category comparison, a zero-baseline chart is clearer. In a timeplot, a narrower labeled vertical range may help show changes, but readers still need to inspect it.
Rounding is different from missing data

Three equal shares rounded to one decimal place become 33.3%,33.3%,33.3%, totaling 99.9%. Explain rounding and calculate chart angles from unrounded values. A large discrepancy should be investigated, not dismissed as rounding.

sections.title: Mode and median: most common versus middle

blocks.text: A descriptive measure is a compact summary of a dataset. Measures of central tendency describe a center or typical value. For categorical data, the mode is especially useful; for ordinal data, we can also find a median.

blocks.alt: The mode is A but the median is B in the same ordered grade dataset.
blocks.caption: The mode is A but the median is B in the same ordered grade dataset.

blocks.text: Mode means most common category
The mode is the category with the highest frequency. It names the tallest bar, widest pie slice, or first category in a descending Pareto chart. Give the category, not just its frequency.
For the lecture list A,A,B,C,A,D,A,B,C,C,A,B,C,D,A, counts are A = 6, B = 3, C = 4, D = 2. The mode is A because 6 is the highest count.
Ties: bimodal and multimodal

When exactly two categories tie for the highest frequency, report both modes: the data are bimodal. If more than two categories tie at the top, report all tied categories: multimodal. The lecture list A,A,B,C,A,C,A,B,C,C,A,C,C,D,A,A,C,D,B has A = 7, C = 7, B = 3, D = 2, so its modes are A and C.
If every category is equally frequent, no category stands out. Many introductory courses call this “no unique mode” or “no mode”. Always state the tie rather than choosing an arbitrary category.
Median requires a meaningful order

The median is the category at the middle of the sorted observations. Nominal blood groups have no meaningful order, so they have no meaningful median. Ordinal grades do: use the grade ranking provided. For these examples, use the order A, B, C, D.

For A,B,B,C,A,D,B,B,A,C,B,B,C,D,A, the counts are A = 4, B = 6, C = 3, D = 2. The sorted list is A,A,A,A,B,B,B,B,B,B,C,C,C,D,D. There are 15 observations, so the middle is position (15+1)/2 = 8. Position 8 is B. The median is B, and the mode is also B.
Even-sized ordinal data
For even n, inspect positions n/2 and n/2 + 1. The lecture’s 14-student example sorts to A,A,A,B,B,B,B,B,B,C,C,C,D,D. Positions 7 and 8 are both B, so the median is unambiguously B.

If the two middle categories differ, do not average their labels or codes. For Poor,Poor,Good,Excellent, the middle categories are Poor and Good. The supplied lecture allows the category on either side of the middle; report both middle categories and follow the course’s requested convention if one answer is required. There is no numerical halfway category justified by ordinal labels.
Mode and median need not agree
For A,B,B,C,A,D,A,B,A,C,B,A,C,D,A, counts are A = 6, B = 4, C = 3, D = 2. Positions 1–6 are A, 7–10 are B, 11–13 are C, and 14–15 are D. The 8th position is B, so the median is B; the mode is A.

blocks.question: 19. A pie chart shows shares 45%,35%,30%. Is this a complete, non-overlapping one-response distribution?
blocks.answer: No. The total is 110%, too far from 100% to be ordinary rounding. Check overlapping responses, wrong denominators or a data error.

blocks.question: 20. Three equal shares are displayed as 33.3% each. Explain the total.
blocks.answer: They total 99.9% because each exact share 1/3 was rounded. The original shares still sum to 1. Calculate from exact counts or unrounded shares.

blocks.question: 21. A picture grows from width 2 cm and height 3 cm to width 4 cm and height 6 cm. How much did its area change?
blocks.answer: Original area = 2×3 = 6 cm². New area = 4×6 = 24 cm², four times as large. It would exaggerate data that only doubled.

blocks.question: 22. With order Poor<Fair<Good<Excellent, responses are Poor,Fair,Good,Good,Excellent. Find mode and median.
blocks.answer: Mode = Good, appearing twice. The 5 observations are already ordered; median is position 3 = Good.

blocks.question: 23. With grade order A,B,C,D, data are A,A,A,A,B,B,C. Find mode and median.
blocks.answer: Mode = A (4 times). Median is position 4 of 7 = A. Do not confuse position 4 with grade D.

blocks.question: 24. Ordered responses are Low,Low,Medium,High. What are the middle categories, and can you average their codes?
blocks.answer: Positions 2 and 3 are Low and Medium. Report both middle categories and follow the course convention if one is requested. Averaging arbitrary codes does not create a meaningful halfway category.

blocks.question: 25. Counts are A=4,B=4,C=2. What are the modes?
blocks.answer: A and B tie for the highest frequency, so both are modes: the data are bimodal. Do not choose one arbitrarily.
